title: A Non-Freaked Out Approach to Reading like a Professional
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart lays out eight personal rules for reading that let a busy teacher keep growing professionally without being overwhelmed by everything there is to read. He separates reading for fun, where rules are suspended, from effective reading, which depends on effort, skill and prior knowledge applied actively and with a precise purpose. Drawing on Adler and Van Doren, he argues for reading most books inspectionally and only a few analytically, often by going straight to the index for what one needs. He adds C. S. Lewis's advice to mix old books with new, a warning against reading to impress others, and the practice of reading an author's whole body of work as a form of mentorship. His capstone is syntopical reading: inspecting many books in pursuit of big questions such as how students best learn, which gives a working knowledge of far more books than reading every word.
points: Stuart argues that effective reading depends on effort, skill and prior knowledge, with effort acting as a multiplier of the other two.
Reading with a specific purpose lets a teacher go to the index or table of contents rather than reading a whole professional book, because "fantastic-ness" is not a useful filter.
He advocates reading everything inspectionally and few things analytically, and favoring older books that have proven staying power.
Reading an author's entire body of work functions as mentorship, giving access to how that person thinks.
Syntopical reading across many books toward big questions maximizes the mind's working "search engine" for professional problems.
quotes: The effectiveness of a reading is dependent, first, on the amount of effort, skill, and prior knowledge I bring to it. Effort is a multiplier of skill and prior knowledge; skill is acquired through deliberate practice; prior knowledge is acquired through reading widely and (in the case of niche-ish books — teacher books, for example) deeply. All of these are “never finished” things — I can always improve the effort I expend, the skill I have, and the knowledge I bring.

Effort, skill, and prior knowledge, like any kind of force, have their greatest effect when applied with precision. Banging a hammer randomly at a board with a nail halfway in it may eventually pound in the nail, but there will be lots of wasted force on the way to the objective.

The whole book is likely fantastic, but living in the 21st century in the most affluent country in the world means that basically everything is fantastic. Fantastic-ness, therefore, is not a good decision-making filter.
It's hard, before reading a book, to even know what purposes to bring to it — and so the first purpose in reading a book must be to inspect it.
This is an Inner Scorecard thing. I think it's beautiful when I speak to someone who I know is well-read, but who doesn't let on about it. Humility is attractive and makes us better, saner teachers.

But I liken reading one or two of a prolific author's books to attending a few of his or her workshops — valuable, but there's not a mentorship relationship there. Yet when I set out to read all of, say, Jim Burke's or C. S. Lewis' books, it's because I want those people in my head and my heart.
When you approach reading in a syntopical fashion, you're able to have a working knowledge of far more books than you would if you opted for the mainstream, “read every word” approach.
